Funnest schools in the World: Education Lessons from Finland

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The “Funnest” Schools in the World

Unique Selling Point:
Imagine a school where the children’s happiness is the teachers’ main concern, where kids are encouraged to explore and be themselves, where play is the basis for learning and where your class and teacher becomes like your family. In Finland that would be any ordinary school.

Summary:
Who would ever use “school” and “fun” in the same sentence? We see how well kids learn in some of the world’s most joyful classrooms. Increasing amounts of information, longer hours, more exams, extra classes, earlier lessons, less play and more work – that is the recipe most education systems are following around the world. In Finland... they do exactly the opposite. And Finnish kids and teachers thrive more than in most schools worldwide.
We experience a day in the life of a Finnish family and see what it is like to attend school where the highest priority seems to be children’s happiness and not test results.

Further information:
Finland has consistently scored among the top countries in the world when it comes to education. Surprisingly, their philosophy is more about letting kids be kids, than to drill and test them. School days are relatively short, kids get little homework, there are almost no exams and children have to play outside every 40 minutes of every single day. Some preschools are even run entirely outdoors in the forest!
What is also amazing about Finland is that there is almost no difference in quality from one school to another and that the gap between the worst and best performing students are relatively insignificant. There are virtually no private schools, and all education is free from preschool to university. Even private schools are by law not allowed to charge fees.
Teachers are also thriving. They are some of the most respected professionals in Finnish society and are seldom stressed or overworked. We go right inside a few Finnish schools to learn the secrets behind a system that manages to make learning fun for both kids and teachers.
On the other hand, South Africa has some of the worst education outcomes in the world and teachers often work under incredible stress. Obviously Finland is a completely different society from South Africa, but are there lessons we can learn from them? A school in Soweto is officially experimenting with the Finnish system and a few other schools have tried to implement some of the Finnish ideas on their own initiative. Is it working and can we find our own unique way to learning success?
The backdrop of our story is the beautiful lake-side cities of Kuopio and Joensuu in Eastern Finland where we will follow the personal story of a Finnish family’s experience of their education system. The youngest ones go to a forest pre-school where they are encouraged to explore mainly through play. Wild tree-climbing and the use of, what many parents might consider dangerous tools, are part of their learning.
Children in Finland only start primary school at age 7. We will see the incredible trust adults put in children, even letting the youngest ones find their own way to school. In the local primary school, we will see the unique relationships between teachers and their students. A teacher can stay with the same group of kids for up to 6 years, forming an almost family-like bond with the children. Teachers have a very high social standing and are some of the most trusted and admired professionals next to doctors.
Even Finnish teenagers are thriving in the local high schools. Instead of high fences and strict controls, Finnish society emphasises openness, trust and inclusivity. In Kuopio the university and university of appled science are on the same campus and share some of their facilities with the vocational high school up the road.
Here is a clip from Michale Moore’s documentary on Finnish schools: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XQ_agxK6fLs

Script:


The “Funnest” Schools in the World
What we can learn from Finland’s education

0. Audio Visuals
1. VO:
If you had a chance to relive your childhood...
Would you want a better report card or more experiences?
Work harder or play harder?
Spend your days indoors studying, or outside exploring?
More time with your family or more time at school?
What is the best direction for a new generation as they prepare for their life journey?
Children montage
2. LINK:
What would the ideal school look like where teachers and learners thrive? Where kids are left to be kids – very little homework and exams not a priority. Where fun is the basis for learning... And yet the results are among the best in the world. Well in one country that would be... just an ordinary school.
Presenter in classroom




3. VO:
Finland is considered one of the least corrupt, safest, wealthiest and socially equal countries in the world - as well as the world’s most literate nation.
Helsinki cut aways

4. VO:
With 4 of their 9 children still at home, Jari & Katriina Koskelo’s family is not exactly the typical household you would expect to find in Finland.
Selina is in the Ninth Grade and excited about her future. Kuopio, Eastern Finland



Family having breakfast & discussing day ahead.
Children greet their parents and head out.
5. I think it is important that everybody has the opportunity to do everything that they want. Selina
6. VO:
Her two younger sisters go to Haapaniemi Primary school. Where mom, Katriina, is a teacher of a class of 27 Grade 3 learners.
Katriina’s children walking to school.
7. Joy motivates me. The joy you see in children learning. Katriina
8. VO:
And joy is exactly what you experience when you step into the school hall, where the children are getting a joint lesson on road safety. It seems like this is a place full of happy children, who want to be here.

Jussi Kukkola is the headmaster. Not that anyone cares about positions.
9. I’m not really the boss, I am more like helping them to succeed.
Jussi

Children walking out of hall
10. VO:
They believe respect lies deeper than titles.
11. They call me by name and I remember almost everyone’s name in my school
Jussi

Children walking out of hall
12. VO:
And this relationship that teachers have with their learners, is foundational.
13.
They are like your parents. You can joke with them and we call them at their first name.

Selina
14. VO:
Every teacher is an educational specialist and often stays with the same class for up to 6 years. They get to know each child’s individual needs, strengths and weaknesses and strong bonds develop between them.
Even though classrooms don’t LOOK very different, the simple principles they use are revolutionary, and go against the rigid teaching traditions used elsewhere.
And according to international tests and surveys, Finland’s schools are some of the top performers and their children some of the happiest in the world.
15. LINK
Incredibly, the gap between the weakest and strongest learners in Finnish schools, is one of the narrowest in the world. There is little difference between the best and worst performing schools, there are few private schools... and by law all education is free.

Presenter CU with children learning in classroom: Blurred background.
16. VO:
A free, nutritious lunch is included every single day – for all children in Finland.
School days are relatively short. Apart from their lunch break, the children already had a 30 minute play break...
but that’s not all...
17. After every 45 min, we have 15 min break – and every break children go outside to play and have fun.
18. VO:
And what about their harsh winters?
19.
Every time they go outside – even if it’s -30!

20. VO:
The Fins also frown upon the idea of homework.
21. We try to focus on working here at school and we give little homework just to practice little bit.

B-roll
22. VO:
Apart from some national tests in grade 6 and 9, the only real exam they write, is the the final one in grade 12. Standardised tests don’t fit into their philosophy. Assessments are done in more informal ways and learners are given very individualised feedback and support.
23. Jussi
I believe that if they get their feedback and support in their learning, they grow and grow and grow and get better all the time. We don’t need those tests.
B-roll
24. VO:
Short days, lots of breaks, little homework, few tests & exams... so how do Finnish children learn then?
25. LINK:
The nature of a child is to want to know new things, to be inquisitive, curious about the world around them and to experiment. Finland’s education system builds on this, taking advantage of children’s natural curiosity and placing it at the heart of how they teach.

Presenter CU with children playing in the background: Blurred background.
26. As a teacher, it’s important how I present new things to children. So that I awaken their curiosity and desire to learn new things. Katriina
27. VO:
For Katriina, like most other Finnish teachers, there is no better classroom than nature!
Here, she lets the children’s curiosity drive them and allow them to explore in a playful way.

In Finnish schools, there are no scripted lessons and no quasi-martial requirements to walk in straight lines or sit up straight.
Their simple secret is that learning is about stimulating and encouraging curiosity.
28. If you experience things from different perspectives, you understand better, so we use play, singing, writing, physical movement...
Katriina
29. VO:
The happiness of a child is paramount. Children are respected as cherished individuals. They are given responsibility, trusted and treated as complete human beings. And their focus is to encourage critical thinking, creativity and simply nurture a love for learning.
To ensure that this happens on a consistent basis in every school, teachers are KEY.
Teaching is one of the highest profile jobs in Finland. It’s one of the hardest University courses to get into and minimum qualification for a teacher, even at Preschool level, is a Masters degree.
This school, right on the campus of the University of Eastern Finland, also acts as a teacher training centre.
30. Every year students have teacher practice here.
So it’s mentored and supervised and we, all staff have special training to do that.
Hilka

B-roll
31. VO:
New ideas are also piloted at these University schools before they are implemented in the rest of the nation’s classrooms.
32. LINK:
You may argue that it’s easy for Finland, as a wealthy nation, to have such a quality education system. The question is... what came first... the wealth or the education?
At school, MS, with blurred background.
33. VO:
Finland has a long history of being a poor, struggling nation. For almost 700 years they suffered oppression by large empires around them...

Making education top priority, was part of their turn-around strategy.
Professor Nadine Peterson of the University of Johannesburg has been to Finland a number of times to learn some of their secrets.

34. my chief learning has been around what do they do to prepare their teachers well Interview Prof Nadine Peterson (UJ)
35. VO:
The Funda Ujabule school in Soweto is a joint venture between the University of Johannesburg and the Gauteng Department of Education and like the Finnish University schools, it’s a teacher training site and educational research laboratory.

Rebecca Maboya is the principal.

One’s immediate impression is that, like in Finnish schools, children seem to want to be here and exude confidence. Presenter arrives at Funda uJabule school
36. The school motto says: You must learn and be joyful.
Interview with a kid
37. in as much as we're teaching these learners, we also become their parents, because they see us as fathers and mothers Rebecca
38. You can sit with them, talk to them about your issues, share with them your stories and they can understand and relate to their personal stories.
39. We need to have a school environment where when learners walk in, they feel at home Rebecca
40. Waarmee eet jy jou pappies? Ka seatla
41. VO:
Laerskool Die Krans in Pretoria, also decided to follow the Finnish model, emphasising experiences, relationships and playful learning.
Vice principal, Adele Havenga, believes school should be a haven from a stressful world and not add extra anxiety.

42. So there's a lot of stress relief and there's there's a lot of just being and being a child once more
Adele
43. It's all about learning through play, it's not about pencil-and-paper tests and being in a rigid learning environment all the time. Prof Nadine
44. VO:
They also believe forcing children to sit still for long hours is unnatural and prevents effective learning.
45. A ten-year-old should actually not sit still for longer than 10 minutes
Adele
46. VO:
Lessons are therefore designed to include regular movement.

Like the Fins, instead of rigid tests, children are assessed in ways that don’t add unnecessary pressure.
47. the teacher will rather say: I'd like to see what you can remember from this week but they were never placed in a situation of being tested.
Adele
48. VO:
And instead of homework, parents and children are encouraged to spend quality time together.
49. All the time that the parent would have would have spent doing homework and stressing about doing homework, rather enjoy your child and be with your child
Adele
50. VO:
In both Die Krans and Funda Ujabule, the idea is not to copy the Finnish model, but to find our own ways to implement some of the principles.


51. So the feedback from high schools are that our learners are willing to try anything, because they’ve never heard the concept of no you cannot do it.
Adele
52. That example is set by a teacher and if your teacher’s attitude is not correct, you would miss that opportunity for children to learn
Prof Nadine
53. They need to walk into teaching and say I am a community builder, this child is looking up to me, I'm a role model
Rebecca
54. Closing LINK:
Maybe one of the most important lessons we can learn from the best schools in the world, is to change our idea of education from producing good scores to creating happy, well-adjusted human beings with a deep hunger to explore and learn more.




Children exploring

A school in Soweto is officially experimenting with the Finnish system and a few other schools have tried to implement some of the Finnish ideas on their own initiative. Is it working and can we find our own unique way to learning success? The backdrop of our story is the beautiful lake-side cities of Kuopio and Joensuu in Eastern Finland where we will follow the personal story of a Finnish family’s experience of their education system. The youngest ones go to a forest pre-school where they are encouraged to explore mainly through play. Wild tree-climbing and the use of, what many parents might consider dangerous tools, are part of their learning. Children in Finland only start primary school at age 7. We will see the incredible trust adults put in children, even letting the youngest ones find their own way to school. In the local primary school, we will see the unique relationships between teachers and their students. A teacher can stay with the same group of kids for up to 6 years, forming an almost family-like bond with the children. Teachers have a very high social standing and are some of the most trusted and admired professionals next to doctors. Even Finnish teenagers are thriving in the local high schools. Instead of high fences and strict controls, Finnish society emphasises openness, trust and inclusivity. In Kuopio the university and university of appled science are on the same campus and share some of their facilities with the vocational high school up the road. Here is a clip from Michale Moore’s documentary on Finnish schools: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XQ_agxK6fLs
